prompt: A `LIST` request is billed at which of the sheet's request prices?
hint: Read the label of the first request line.

choices.text: The `GET` price, 0.00056 a thousand, since a listing only reads
choices.why: It reads, and it is still billed with `PUT`, `COPY` and `POST`.

choices.text: The `PUT` price, 0.00700 a thousand
choices.why: Right. The sheet's line is "PUT, COPY, POST, LIST".

choices.text: Nothing: listing is free
choices.why: Only data coming in is free.

choices.text: Per GB of keys returned
choices.why: A request is priced per request, whatever it returns.

prompt: What does the sheet charge for data coming into S3 from the internet?
hint: Read the last line of the transfer block.

choices.text: 0.15000 a GB, the same as going out
choices.why: That is the price of the first tier going out.

choices.text: 0.01000 a GB, like a zone crossing
choices.why: That is the price between zones.

choices.text: Nothing, 0.00000
choices.why: Right, which is why a bucket fills cheaply and empties expensively; the `PUT` requests that write it are still billed.

choices.text: It depends on the storage class written to
choices.why: Transfer in has one price, and the class changes storage and retrieval.

prompt: At 0.04050 USD per GB-month and 0.00056 USD per 1,000 GETs, how many GET requests cost the same as storing 1 GB for a month? Round to the nearest whole number.
Where do the request counts in this lesson's arithmetic come from?

choices.text: From moto's request log
choices.why: moto prints one line per request and meters nothing; no figure here comes from it.

choices.text: From the bill of the account the lesson was recorded on
choices.why: There is no account and no bill in this course.

choices.text: From the design: counts chosen to describe it, multiplied by the sheet
choices.why: Right. They are the design's counts, not measurements of anything that ran.

choices.text: From CloudWatch metrics of the bucket
choices.why: Those exist on AWS, and nothing in this lab produces them.

prompt: The dashboard's month is 47.91 USD and the same bytes in 123 files cost 0.31. What changed between the two?

choices.text: The storage class
choices.why: Both rows price Standard.

choices.text: The number of requests, since a request costs the same whatever its size
choices.why: Right. Two million objects read daily against 123 files read daily.

choices.text: The number of bytes stored
choices.why: Both store the same 7.63 GB.

choices.text: Transfer out
choices.why: Both rows send nothing out of the region.

prompt: Writing 2,000,000 objects at 0.00700 USD per 1,000 PUT requests costs how many USD?
Which of these produce many small objects? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A stream writer flushing whatever arrived in the last few seconds
choices.why: Yes: a file per flush.

choices.text: A prefix per hour per customer
choices.why: Yes: partitions too fine for the data.

choices.text: One object per app event
choices.why: Yes: convenient to write and ruinous to read.

choices.text: A nightly job compacting the day into 64 MB files
choices.why: That is the cure, not the cause.

prompt: Quitanda moves its 4 KB events to Glacier Instant Retrieval to save on storage, and the dashboard keeps reading them every morning. What happens to the bill?
hint: Size billed, and the price of each read.

choices.text: It falls, by the ratio of the storage prices
choices.why: Storage was 0.31 of 47.91; the reads are what grow.

choices.text: It rises: each event billed as 128 KB, each read dearer
choices.why: Right. Each GET costs almost eighteen times as much, plus a fee per GB read: small objects are punished twice by an archive class.

choices.text: It stays the same, since a request costs the same in every class
choices.why: The sheet prints 0.01000 for a Glacier Instant Retrieval GET against 0.00056.

choices.text: The dashboard stops working until the events are restored
choices.why: Instant Retrieval needs no restore; it is read in milliseconds.

prompt: Using the four tiers (0.15000 for the first 10,240 GB, 0.13800 for the next 40,960), what does sending 15,360 GB to the internet in one month cost, in USD?
hint: 10,240 at the first price, the rest at the second.

prompt: Why does the CloudFront line of `reads.py` print a dash for transfer and total?

choices.text: Because transfer to CloudFront is free, so there is nothing to print
choices.why: Free would print 0.00; the dash is for a price the sheet does not have.

choices.text: Because the cache ratio is unknown
choices.why: The program assumes 95 in 100; the gap is a price, not a ratio.

choices.text: Because CloudFront's delivery price is in an offer the sheet does not read
choices.why: Right. The line shows S3's half and leaves the rest unpriced rather than guessed.

choices.text: Because moto does not implement CloudFront
choices.why: The program runs no moto at all; it multiplies prices by counts.

prompt: Besides the bill, what does putting CloudFront in front of the image bucket change?

choices.text: The bucket can stay private, readable only by CloudFront
choices.why: Right. The internet talks to CloudFront, and the bucket keeps its Block Public Access.

choices.text: The images move to the edge locations for good, so the bucket can be emptied
choices.why: The edge keeps copies; the bucket stays the origin it fetches from.

choices.text: The bucket must become public for CloudFront to read it
choices.why: It is the reverse: a bucket policy lets CloudFront in and nobody else.

choices.text: Nothing beyond the bill
choices.why: The lesson names a second effect that matters as much.

prompt: A Spark job in one zone of São Paulo reads 2 TB from an S3 bucket in São Paulo, through a gateway endpoint. What transfer does it pay?
hint: S3 is regional, and the endpoint is free.

choices.text: 2,048 × 0.01000, for crossing a zone
choices.why: The zone charge is between your own resources; S3 is regional.

choices.text: 2,048 × 0.0930, for the NAT gateway
choices.why: The endpoint sends the traffic past the NAT gateway.

choices.text: None; only the requests are billed
choices.why: Right. Same region, through a free endpoint.

choices.text: 2,048 × 0.15000, for leaving S3
choices.why: That price is for leaving AWS to the internet.

prompt: A ___ endpoint for S3 costs nothing and lets machines in a private subnet reach S3 with no charge per GB processed.
A database replicates 500 GB a month to a standby in another zone. Why is the transfer 10.00 and not 5.00?
hint: Read the sheet's label for the zone line.

choices.text: The zone price doubles after the first 250 GB
choices.why: The zone price has no tiers in the sheet.

choices.text: Each GB is charged leaving one zone and again entering the other
choices.why: Right. The line says "each direction": 500 × 0.01000 × 2.

choices.text: Replication traffic also pays the NAT gateway's charge for every GB
choices.why: Traffic between zones of one VPC does not pass a NAT gateway.

choices.text: Multi-AZ always keeps two standbys
choices.why: The example has one standby; the doubling is the price's direction.

prompt: On a requester-pays bucket, who pays for the storage?

choices.text: The requester, in proportion to what it reads
choices.why: Requesters pay for requests and transfer only.

choices.text: The owner
choices.why: Right. Requester pays moves requests and transfer, not storage.

choices.text: Nobody: storage is free on such a bucket
choices.why: Storage is billed as on any bucket.

choices.text: AWS, as part of the open data programme
choices.why: The lesson names no such thing; storage stays with the owner.

prompt: Quitanda wants its public product images on a requester-pays bucket, so that viewers pay the transfer. Why can that not work?
hint: Whom would S3 bill for an anonymous request?

choices.text: Requester pays applies only to Glacier classes
choices.why: It applies to the bucket, whatever the class.

choices.text: Requester pays is limited to 10 TB a month of transfer per bucket
choices.why: There is no such limit in the lesson; the obstacle is who can be billed.

choices.text: Anonymous requests are refused, as there is nobody to bill
choices.why: Right. A requester-pays bucket cannot also serve the public.

choices.text: Images must be served through CloudFront, not straight from a bucket
choices.why: Nothing requires it; it is the requester-pays rule that blocks this.

prompt: Of the lesson's changes, which takes the most off a bill for the least effort, according to the lesson?

choices.text: Moving the lake to us-east-1, where prices are lower
choices.why: The copy alone is 706.56, and the data usually has to stay in Brazil.

choices.text: A gateway endpoint for S3
choices.why: Right. It costs nothing and removed 190.46 a month of NAT processing in the example.

choices.text: Requester pays on every bucket Quitanda's own teams read
choices.why: The charges would move between Quitanda's own accounts and nothing would be saved.

choices.text: Rewriting the dashboard to read Parquet
choices.why: Compaction saves on requests and takes work; the lesson calls the endpoint the cheapest change.
